title: Human Physiology & Anatomy — Systems, Homeostasis & Integration

subChunks.title: Human Physiology & Anatomy — Systems, Homeostasis & Integration

storyBeats.txt: Theodora placed her hand over her heart and was quiet for a moment. "Seventy times a minute," she said. "One hundred thousand beats per day. Thirty-five million per year. The heart has been beating in your chest since before you were born, without instruction, without pause — a pump so reliable that its failure is the event by which we define death."

"The body is not a collection of parts. It is a system of systems, each monitoring the others, each sending signals and receiving responses. The internal environment is kept extraordinarily stable — temperature, pH, blood glucose, osmolarity — within narrow ranges despite enormous variation in what you eat, how hard you exercise, and what the external world throws at you. That stability is homeostasis, and it is one of the most impressive feats of biological engineering."

"Understanding human physiology is understanding yourself. Every moment of consciousness, every breath, every immune response, every thought is a biological event with a mechanism. And when those mechanisms fail — in disease — understanding physiology is the foundation of medicine."

subChunks.hookHtml: Human physiology is the study of how the body works — how its cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems perform their functions and interact to sustain life. Central to physiology is the concept of homeostasis: the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external fluctuations. The body achieves this through negative feedback loops in which deviations from set-points trigger corrective responses. Pathology — disease — is often the failure of these homeostatic mechanisms. Understanding physiology is the scientific foundation of medicine.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Homeostasis and Feedback

Negative feedback: The most common homeostatic mechanism. A change in a variable is detected by a receptor/sensor; the information is sent to a control centre; an effector responds to reverse the change. Example: body temperature rises → hypothalamus detects change → sweating and vasodilation → temperature falls back toward 37°C.

Positive feedback: Amplifies a deviation rather than reversing it. Used for processes requiring rapid completion. Example: childbirth — stretching of the cervix → oxytocin release → stronger contractions → more stretching → more oxytocin → delivery. Blood clotting cascade is also positive feedback.

The Cardiovascular System

The heart is a double pump: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body (systemic circulation). The heart muscle is cardiac muscle — involuntary, striated, and connected by gap junctions allowing coordinated contraction.

The cardiac cycle: Diastole (filling) → atrial systole → ventricular systole → diastole. Heart sounds (lub-dub) are caused by valve closure (atrioventricular then semilunar valves). Resting heart rate ≈70 bpm; cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (≈5 L/min at rest).

Blood pressure: Systolic (ventricular contraction) / diastolic (relaxation). Normal ≈120/80 mmHg. Regulated by cardiac output and peripheral resistance (vessel diameter and blood viscosity).

Blood vessels: Arteries (thick walls, elastic, high pressure), arterioles (control distribution via vasoconstriction/vasodilation), capillaries (one cell thick — exchange of gases, nutrients, waste), venules, veins (low pressure, large lumen, valves prevent backflow).

Blood composition: Plasma (55%) — water, dissolved proteins, ions, nutrients, hormones, waste. Red blood cells (44%) — no nucleus; packed with haemoglobin for O₂ transport. White blood cells — immune defence. Platelets — clotting.

The Respiratory System

Gas exchange occurs in alveoli — thin-walled, richly vascularised air sacs maximising surface area (≈70 m²). O₂ diffuses from alveoli (high pO₂) into blood; CO₂ diffuses from blood (high pCO₂) into alveoli — both by Fick's Law of Diffusion (rate ∝ area × concentration gradient / thickness).

Breathing (ventilation) is driven by pressure differences. Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and flattens → thoracic volume increases → pressure drops → air flows in. Expiration: diaphragm relaxes → volume decreases → pressure rises → air flows out.

CO₂ is transported mainly as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in plasma; O₂ mainly bound to haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin). CO₂ indirectly regulates breathing: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Rising CO₂ → falling blood pH → detected by chemoreceptors → increased ventilation rate.

The Nervous System

Divisions: Central NS (brain + spinal cord) — integration. Peripheral NS — sensory (afferent) neurons carry signals to CNS; motor (efferent) neurons carry signals from CNS. Motor NS divides into somatic (voluntary — skeletal muscle) and autonomic (involuntary — cardiac, smooth muscle, glands). Autonomic: sympathetic ("fight or flight" — increases heart rate, dilates pupils, inhibits digestion) and parasympathetic ("rest and digest" — decreases heart rate, stimulates digestion).

Action potential: Electrical signal along a neuron. Resting membrane potential ≈−70 mV (more negative inside — due to K⁺ leaking out and Na⁺/K⁺ pump). Depolarisation: Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ rushes in → membrane potential rises to ≈+40 mV. Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels close; K⁺ channels open → K⁺ flows out → potential returns to rest. All-or-nothing law: if threshold is reached, full action potential fires; below threshold, nothing. Speed enhanced by myelin sheaths (saltatory conduction in nodes of Ranvier).

Synaptic transmission: Action potential reaches axon terminal → Ca²⁺ influx → neurotransmitter vesicles fuse with membrane → neurotransmitter released into synaptic cleft → binds postsynaptic receptors → postsynaptic potential generated.

The Endocrine System

Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood, affecting distant target organs. Slower than nervous signalling but longer-lasting.

Key hormones: Insulin (pancreatic β cells) — lowers blood glucose (promotes uptake and storage). Glucagon (pancreatic α cells) — raises blood glucose. Adrenaline (adrenal medulla) — fight-or-flight response. Cortisol (adrenal cortex) — stress response, anti-inflammatory. Thyroid hormones (T₃/T₄) — regulate metabolic rate. ADH (antidiuretic hormone, posterior pituitary) — regulates water reabsorption in kidney.

Blood glucose homeostasis: A classic negative feedback. Blood glucose rises after a meal → insulin released → cells take up glucose → glucose stored as glycogen in liver and muscle → blood glucose falls. If blood glucose falls → glucagon released → glycogen broken down → glucose released → blood glucose rises. Failure: Type 1 diabetes (autoimmune destruction of β cells; no insulin); Type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance).

The Kidney and Excretion

The kidney filters ≈180 L of blood per day through glomeruli (ultrafiltration), then reabsorbs most water, glucose, and ions in the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, and distal tubule, leaving concentrated waste (urea, excess ions) as urine (≈1.5 L/day). ADH controls water reabsorption in the collecting duct — high ADH → concentrated urine; low ADH → dilute urine. Aldosterone controls Na⁺ reabsorption.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how the body keeps blood glucose stable after a large meal — walk through the hormones involved, where they come from, and why this is a negative feedback loop.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A patient presents with persistent high blood pressure (hypertension: >140/90 mmHg). (1) Define systolic and diastolic blood pressure in terms of the cardiac cycle. (2) Identify two physiological variables that determine blood pressure and explain how each could cause hypertension if dysregulated. (3) The patient is prescribed a beta-blocker (reduces heart rate) and an ACE inhibitor (reduces vasoconstriction, lowering peripheral resistance). Predict the physiological effect of each drug on blood pressure and explain the mechanism. (4) The patient is also told to reduce dietary salt (sodium chloride). Explain the physiological chain from high salt intake to elevated blood pressure. (5) Uncontrolled hypertension damages arteries over time. Explain how chronic high pressure causes arterial wall damage and why this increases stroke and heart attack risk.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Systolic pressure: the maximum pressure in arteries during ventricular systole (contraction) — when the ventricles contract and eject blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery. Diastolic pressure: the minimum pressure during ventricular diastole (relaxation/filling) — maintained by elastic recoil of the aorta wall. Normal ≈120 mmHg systolic / 80 mmHg diastolic.

(2) Blood pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (BP = CO × TPR). (a) Increased cardiac output: caused by increased heart rate (sympathetic activation, hyperthyroidism) or increased stroke volume (fluid overload, increased preload). Excess blood volume from high salt intake → increased venous return → increased stroke volume → higher CO → higher BP. (b) Increased peripheral resistance: caused by vasoconstriction (sympathetic nervous system, angiotensin II), atherosclerosis (plaques narrow arteries, increasing resistance), or increased blood viscosity. Either mechanism elevates BP.

(3) Beta-blocker (e.g. atenolol): blocks β₁-adrenergic receptors on the heart → reduces sympathetic stimulation → decreases heart rate and decreases force of contraction → lower cardiac output → lower blood pressure. ACE inhibitor (e.g. lisinopril): blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulator of aldosterone). With ACE inhibited: less angiotensin II → less vasoconstriction → lower peripheral resistance → lower BP; also less aldosterone → less Na⁺/water retention → lower blood volume → lower CO.

(4) High salt (NaCl) intake → raised plasma Na⁺ concentration → osmoreceptors in hypothalamus detect increased osmolarity → increased ADH release → increased water reabsorption from renal collecting duct → increased blood volume. Also: aldosterone-independent: raised Na⁺ directly causes water retention. Increased blood volume → increased venous return → increased cardiac output → elevated blood pressure. Kidneys also respond by retaining more Na⁺ (pressure natriuresis: normally, high BP causes kidneys to excrete Na⁺/water; if this mechanism is impaired, hypertension is sustained).

(5) Chronic high pressure mechanically stresses arterial endothelium (inner lining). Damage triggers an inflammatory response and lipid infiltration → atherosclerotic plaque formation (fatty streaks → fibrous plaques). Plaques narrow the arterial lumen (increasing resistance and turbulence), reduce elasticity, and create rough surfaces prone to thrombosis. If a plaque ruptures: platelet aggregation and clot formation. Clot in a coronary artery → myocardial infarction (heart attack). Clot in a cerebral artery, or weakened vessel bursting → stroke. High pressure also causes hypertrophy (thickening) of the left ventricle (working harder to pump against resistance) → left ventricular failure over time.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: During vigorous exercise, the body's demand for oxygen increases dramatically. (1) List four physiological changes that occur in the cardiovascular and respiratory systems during exercise and explain the homeostatic purpose of each. (2) Body temperature rises during exercise. Describe two mechanisms by which the body loses heat and explain the negative feedback loop that controls them. (3) Blood pH falls during intense exercise (lactic acid and CO₂ production). How does the body detect and respond to this acidosis? What are the short-term and medium-term responses? (4) After prolonged exercise, blood glucose may fall. Explain the hormonal response that restores blood glucose and how the liver is involved. (5) An athlete's training over months increases stroke volume (the heart pumps more blood per beat). Explain how this adaptation allows the athlete to achieve the same cardiac output at a lower resting heart rate — and why this is physiologically beneficial.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Four changes during exercise: (a) Heart rate increases (sympathetic NS releases adrenaline → chronotropic effect): delivers more blood per minute to working muscles. (b) Stroke volume increases (increased venous return due to muscle pump, increased preload → Starling's Law): further increases cardiac output. (c) Vasodilation in skeletal muscle arterioles (local metabolite accumulation — CO₂, H⁺, adenosine): redirects blood flow to active muscles; vasoconstriction in non-essential beds (digestive). (d) Respiratory rate and tidal volume increase (detected by chemoreceptors sensing rising CO₂/falling pH): removes CO₂ faster and delivers more O₂.

(2) Heat loss mechanisms: (a) Sweating: eccrine sweat glands produce sweat → evaporation cools the skin surface (uses latent heat of vaporisation). (b) Vasodilation of skin arterioles: more blood flows to skin surface → heat dissipated by radiation and convection. Negative feedback: hypothalamus (thermoregulatory centre) detects blood temperature rising above 37°C → signals sweat glands to increase secretion and signals skin arterioles to dilate → heat lost → body temperature falls back to set point → signals reduce. Peripheral thermoreceptors provide additional anticipatory input.

(3) Acidosis detection and response: chemoreceptors in the medulla (central) and carotid/aortic bodies (peripheral) detect rising CO₂ and falling pH. Short-term: ventilation rate and depth increase dramatically → CO₂ blown off faster → pH rises. Medium-term (minutes to hours): kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻ excretion/retention — if acidosis persists, kidneys retain HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) and excrete H⁺ in urine, restoring blood pH toward 7.4. Blood bicarbonate buffer system: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H₂O + CO₂ — immediately buffers pH changes; expired CO₂ shifts the equilibrium left, removing acid.

(4) Falling blood glucose → decreased insulin, increased glucagon release from pancreatic α cells. Glucagon acts on liver hepatocytes: activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate → glucose → released into blood). If glycogen stores are depleted: glucagon + cortisol promote gluconeogenesis (synthesis of glucose from amino acids, lactate, glycerol). Adrenaline also stimulates glycogenolysis in liver and muscle. Result: blood glucose rises back toward ≈4–6 mmol/L — classic negative feedback.

(5) Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. If stroke volume increases (due to training-induced cardiac hypertrophy — larger ventricular chamber, stronger ventricular walls, greater filling volume), the same cardiac output can be maintained with a lower heart rate. Trained athletes often have resting heart rates of 40–55 bpm (bradycardia) vs ≈70 bpm in untrained individuals. Benefits: (a) Lower heart rate means longer diastolic filling time — better coronary perfusion (coronary arteries fill during diastole). (b) Cardiac muscle has more time to rest between contractions — reduced mechanical stress, lower oxygen demand at rest. (c) Greater cardiac reserve: during maximal exercise, trained athletes can increase heart rate dramatically from a lower resting level, achieving much higher peak cardiac output. (d) Reduced risk of arrhythmias and ischemia at rest.
learningObjectives: Explain negative and positive feedback homeostatic mechanisms with specific physiological examples including blood glucose regulation and temperature control.
Describe the structure and function of the cardiovascular system, including the cardiac cycle, blood pressure regulation, and gas exchange in capillaries.
Explain how action potentials are generated and propagated, and how synaptic transmission links neurons to each other and to effectors.
Describe the endocrine regulation of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon, and identify the physiological consequences of diabetes mellitus.
commonMistakes: Confusing arteries and veins by oxygen content rather than direction — arteries carry blood away from the heart (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood); veins carry blood toward the heart (the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood).

Treating nerve impulses as electrical current — action potentials are electrochemical signals involving ion movements across membranes, not electrons flowing along a wire; they travel in one direction only and have a refractory period.

Forgetting that insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it — confusing these two antagonistic hormones is common; both are produced in the pancreas but by different cell types (β vs α cells) and have opposite effects.

Describing breathing as simply 'pulling air in' — ventilation is driven by pressure differences generated by volume changes; the diaphragm contracts to increase thoracic volume, reducing pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in down the pressure gradient.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly describes a negative feedback loop with receptor, control centre, effector, and corrective response for a specific physiological variable.
Accurately traces the path of blood through the heart, lungs, and body, and explains gas exchange at alveoli and capillaries.
Explains action potential generation using ion movements (Na⁺ influx, K⁺ efflux) and correctly applies the all-or-nothing law.
Describes blood glucose homeostasis quantitatively (hormones, target organs, effects) and identifies at least two physiological consequences of insulin deficiency.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The force of ventricular contraction increases with increasing end-diastolic volume (preload) — within physiological limits, the more blood fills the ventricle during diastole, the stronger the subsequent contraction and the greater the stroke volume. This intrinsic cardiac mechanism allows the heart to automatically match output to venous return, ensuring equal pumping by the left and right ventricles without neural input.

A hormonal cascade regulating blood pressure and fluid balance. Low blood pressure → kidney juxtaglomerular cells release renin → renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE converts to angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone release from adrenal cortex → Na⁺ retention → water retention → increased blood volume and pressure. RAAS is a major target of antihypertensive drugs.

The synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre. Acetylcholine (ACh) released from the motor neuron terminal crosses the synaptic cleft and binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end plate, generating a motor end plate potential that triggers an action potential in the muscle fibre and initiates contraction. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease targeting these receptors; curare and nerve agents disrupt NMJ function.

A highly selective permeability barrier formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte foot processes and pericytes. The BBB maintains brain ionic homeostasis and excludes pathogens and toxins, but also blocks most drugs — a major challenge in treating CNS diseases. Lipid-soluble molecules (including alcohol, general anaesthetics) cross readily; glucose and amino acids are transported by specific carriers; proteins and most hydrophilic drugs are excluded.

At high altitude, reduced pO₂ triggers hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1) in kidney cells, stimulating erythropoietin (EPO) production. EPO acts on bone marrow to increase red blood cell production (erythropoiesis) — raising haematocrit and O₂-carrying capacity. Altitude training exploits this adaptation. Synthetic EPO is banned in sport because it artificially enhances O₂ delivery. HIF-1α research led to a Nobel Prize in 2019.

questions.questionHtml: A patient with Type 1 diabetes has destroyed pancreatic β cells. Which of the following correctly describes the immediate physiological consequence of eating a carbohydrate-rich meal without an insulin injection?
options: Blood glucose will fall rapidly because glucagon will be over-produced
Blood glucose will rise and remain elevated because without insulin, cells cannot take up glucose efficiently and the liver does not store excess glucose as glycogen
Blood glucose will normalise because the liver will automatically convert excess glucose to glycogen without requiring insulin
Blood glucose will fall below normal because the kidneys will excrete all excess glucose
questions.correctAnswer: Blood glucose will rise and remain elevated because without insulin, cells cannot take up glucose efficiently and the liver does not store excess glucose as glycogen
questions.explanationHtml: Insulin is required for: (1) translocation of GLUT4 glucose transporters to the cell surface in muscle and adipose tissue — without insulin, these cells cannot take up glucose efficiently; (2) activation of glycogen synthase in the liver — without insulin, glucose is not stored as glycogen; (3) inhibition of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Without insulin after a meal: absorbed glucose accumulates in the blood (hyperglycaemia). Blood glucose may reach 15–25 mmol/L (normal fasting ≈4–6 mmol/L). The kidneys reabsorb glucose up to a maximum (renal threshold ≈10 mmol/L); above this, glucose spills into urine (glycosuria) — an osmotic diuretic causing excessive urination (polyuria) and thirst (polydipsia). If untreated, fat breakdown for energy produces ketone bodies → diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.questionHtml: During a sprint, lactic acid builds up in muscle. A student explains: 'When blood pH falls, chemoreceptors detect this and send signals to increase breathing rate, removing CO₂ and raising pH.' Is this explanation complete and accurate?
options: Yes — this is a complete account of how exercise acidosis is corrected
Partially — the student correctly describes the ventilatory response, but omits the bicarbonate buffer system that immediately resists pH change, and the renal response that restores HCO₃⁻ over hours
No — CO₂, not pH, is the primary stimulus for breathing; pH changes from lactic acid do not affect ventilation
No — the response is positive feedback, not negative feedback; pH falls → more lactic acid → more pH fall
questions.correctAnswer: Partially — the student correctly describes the ventilatory response, but omits the bicarbonate buffer system that immediately resists pH change, and the renal response that restores HCO₃⁻ over hours
questions.explanationHtml: The student's account is correct but incomplete. Three defence systems act in sequence: (1) Immediate chemical buffering: blood bicarbonate (H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂) minimises pH change instantly — without this buffer, pH would crash catastrophically. (2) Ventilatory response (seconds-minutes): chemoreceptors detect both rising CO₂ and falling pH (H⁺); increased breathing removes CO₂, driving the buffer equilibrium to the right and consuming H⁺. The student describes this correctly. (3) Renal response (hours-days): kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻ excretion/reabsorption and H⁺ secretion to restore buffer capacity. For acute exercise acidosis this is less relevant, but for chronic conditions (renal tubular acidosis, chronic respiratory disease) renal compensation is critical. Option C is incorrect — while CO₂ is the dominant driver of resting ventilation, pH changes from lactic acid (metabolic acidosis) do stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) and contribute to exercise hyperpnoea.

questions.questionHtml: A patient is given atropine, which blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (the receptors for the parasympathetic nervous system's neurotransmitter). Which combination of effects would you predict?
options: Decreased heart rate, increased digestion, constricted pupils — blocking parasympathetic effects means parasympathetic actions are removed
Increased heart rate, decreased digestion, dilated pupils — blocking parasympathetic receptors removes the 'rest and digest' brake, allowing sympathetic tone to dominate
No effect on heart rate; digestive effects only
Increased heart rate and increased digestion — atropine stimulates both branches of the autonomic nervous system simultaneously
questions.correctAnswer: Increased heart rate, decreased digestion, dilated pupils — blocking parasympathetic receptors removes the 'rest and digest' brake, allowing sympathetic tone to dominate
questions.explanationHtml: The autonomic nervous system operates via dual innervation: most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs that oppose each other. At rest, the parasympathetic system dominates the heart (vagal tone slows heart rate) and promotes digestion. Atropine blocks muscarinic (parasympathetic) receptors: (a) Heart: parasympathetic slowing is removed → heart rate increases (tachycardia — used in bradycardia/asystole treatment and to prevent reflex bradycardia during anaesthesia). (b) Digestion: parasympathetic stimulation of gut motility and secretion is blocked → decreased gut motility (constipation), dry mouth (reduced salivary secretion). (c) Eyes: parasympathetic constricts the pupil (miosis via sphincter pupillae); blocking this → pupil dilated (mydriasis — used by ophthalmologists). Atropine is used in medicine as an antidote to organophosphate poisoning (which causes excess ACh by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase) and as a premedication before surgery.
